text:
Prospective, triple-blinded, parallel-group randomized controlled superiority trial investigating weight-based dosing of ondansetron to reduce hypotension after spinal anesthesia for cesarean section. 228 pregnant women were randomized; 215 remained for intention-to-treat analysis after exclusions.

Intervention. Intravenous ondansetron given 5 minutes before induction of spinal anesthesia at one of three weight-based doses: normal saline (group NS, n=72), ondansetron 0.05 mg/kg (group O1, n=71), or ondansetron 0.1 mg/kg (group O2, n=72).

Hypotension outcomes. The incidence of hypotension was 81.9% in the saline group, 84.5% in the 0.05 mg/kg group, and 73.6% in the 0.1 mg/kg group (p=0.23) — no statistically significant difference between groups. The number of hypotensive episodes before delivery (first 14 minutes after spinal anesthesia) was significantly higher in the 0.05 mg/kg group than in saline (5 versus 2 episodes, p=0.02).

Other outcomes. Overall heart rates throughout the operations did not differ among groups. Ephedrine requirements and amount of blood loss were similar across groups. The metoclopramide (antiemetic rescue) requirement was significantly lower in the 0.1 mg/kg group compared with saline (2.8% versus 16.7%, p=0.01). There were no serious adverse events in maternal or neonatal complications.

Conclusion. In this trial, weight-based ondansetron at 0.05 or 0.1 mg/kg did not significantly reduce the incidence of hypotension following spinal anesthesia for cesarean section, although the 0.1 mg/kg dose reduced the need for rescue antiemetic. The doses reported (0.05 mg/kg and 0.1 mg/kg IV) are the trial interventions, not a clinical recommendation; ondansetron is not established as a hypotension prophylaxis agent and standard vasopressor-based management remains the mainstay.
title: Minimal effective weight-based dosing of ondansetron to reduce hypotension in cesarean section under spinal anesthesia: a randomized controlled trial
